title: Competitive Wine Tasting

jokes.text: PA announcement offers horseback riding, water skiing, fencing — funded by getting enough people to pay to learn hopscotch
jokes.setup: Greendale advertises aspirational, expensive-sounding elective classes
jokes.punchline: The whole thing is contingent on enough people paying for hopscotch — revealing the school's absurd financial desperation
jokes.explanation: Classic Community cold-open worldbuilding joke. The absurdist fiscal logic (hopscotch funding fencing) efficiently establishes Greendale's institutional dysfunction. Clean structure, character-consistent for the school.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: I took a joke-writing class once. Dropped after learning setups.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: So a priest, a rabbi, and a minister walk into a bar...

jokes.text: "Oh, they've got a class on how to write jokes. / Oh, don't take that. / I dropped it after the lesson on setups. / The Professor is so old..."
jokes.setup: Someone notices a joke-writing class on the board and another character warns against it
jokes.punchline: They dropped it after the lesson on setups — and then immediately begin demonstrating a half-finished 'The Professor is so old...' setup, never delivering the punchline, meta-commenting on bad joke structure
jokes.explanation: Genuinely exceptional meta-comedy. The joke IS the structural incompleteness — dropping the class after learning setups means they can begin 'The Professor is so old...' but have no punchline. It's a joke about bad joke-writing that is itself a brilliantly constructed joke. The form enacts the content. This is the kind of layered self-awareness Community does better than almost any show.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You know, when I was your age, I learned that the key to a fulfilling education is choosing the right... electives.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You want to make sure you're getting the most out of your time, if you know what I mean. Really... stretch yourself. Try new positions.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: And always remember: it's not about the size of your course load, it's about how you... apply yourself.

jokes.text: "I'll give you the same advice my father gave me the night I lost my virginity. 'Just pick one. They all cost the same.'"
jokes.setup: Someone is overwhelmed by elective choices; Pierce offers paternal wisdom
jokes.punchline: The fatherly advice was about choosing a prostitute, recontextualized as class selection
jokes.explanation: Very well constructed misdirection. The dual-reading is clean — the advice literally works for class selection AND reveals Pierce's seedy backstory simultaneously. The 'They all cost the same' line does heavy lifting. Classic Pierce: casually horrifying but delivered as wisdom.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So you two are taking an acting class to tap into your emotional cores?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I figured you'd both prefer to just go play foosball or something.

jokes.text: Britta explains she and Troy are taking acting to 'tap into emotional cores.' Jeff: 'Hmm. Foosball was full?' Troy: 'I'm on the wait list.'
jokes.setup: Britta gives an earnest, pretentious explanation for why she and Troy are taking an acting class together
jokes.punchline: Jeff dismisses the whole rationale with a dismissive quip; Troy's sincere confirmation that foosball was his first choice undercuts Britta's pretension even further
jokes.explanation: Two-beat joke that works both times. Jeff's snark punctures Britta's pretentiousness efficiently, then Troy's earnest confirmation that foosball was indeed his first choice doubles the laugh. Both characters land exactly as written.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I got into the media class! I'm so excited!

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: It's an entire academic course analyzing one sitcom.

jokes.text: "'Who Indeed: A Critical Analysis of Television's Who's the Boss?' The professor of this class is the author of this book. / 'We got him? / I know.'"
jokes.setup: Abed shows off his elective choice — an entire academic course devoted to analyzing the TV show Who's the Boss?
jokes.punchline: The genuine excitement about landing the author-professor, delivered with the reverence you'd give a Nobel laureate, makes the absurdity land through pure character sincerity
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Abed. The joke isn't that the class exists — it's that Abed treats the author with the awe of a child meeting a rock star. The 'We got him? / I know.' exchange is a micro-masterpiece of character economy. It also sets up the entire Who's the Boss? subplot.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Jeff, we're taking a wine class together! It's going to be amazing!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm going to look up how to laugh in Italian so I can do it convincingly when you talk about the notes.

jokes.text: "While you knuckleheads are expanding your minds and souls, I'll be expanding my liver in 'Italian Wine Tasting.'"
jokes.setup: Everyone shares their aspirational elective choices
jokes.punchline: Jeff reframes self-indulgent drinking as a rational alternative to self-improvement
jokes.explanation: Solid Jeff joke. The parallel structure ('expanding your minds... expanding my liver') is clean and character-consistent. Not surprising but executed well.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I've got extensive legal experience with wine. I've helped a lot of wealthy people avoid justice.

jokes.text: Pierce says he has a wine cellar. Shirley clarifies. Pierce: 'And it's ha ha.' Then: 'Anyone can have a cellar. It's what's in it that counts.' Shirley: 'Pierce's has a special gym with swings and saddles.'
jokes.setup: Pierce brags about his wine cellar and corrects the Italian pronunciation of 'ha ha'
jokes.punchline: Shirley reveals the cellar contains a 'special gym with swings and saddles' — the wine cellar is a sex dungeon
jokes.explanation: Good two-beat joke. The setup about the wine cellar primes for wine snobbery; the pivot to sexual apparatus is a solid misdirect. Pierce's immediate deflection ('we don't discuss the special gym') adds a third beat that extends the laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: So what's in your wine cellar anyway?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Only the finest vintages, Troy. Bottles worth thousands.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wow, do you ever just go down there and... get it up?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: What? No! Troy, that's not— we're talking about wine!

jokes.text: "Hmm. How do you say 'ha ha' in Italian? / I'll look it up."
jokes.setup: Britta is delighted that Jeff is taking Italian Wine Tasting; Jeff's condescending about Pierce also taking the class
jokes.punchline: Pierce literally looks up the Italian translation of 'ha ha' rather than engaging with the insult — suggesting he has the last laugh and doesn't care, or is too oblivious to recognize the slight
jokes.explanation: Good beat. The joke works on two levels: Pierce is either genuinely oblivious to the insult, or he is responding to it with cheerful deflection. Either reading is funny given his character. The literalism of actually looking it up is a nice touch.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I'm taking wine class because I want to learn about wine and expand my palate.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Just kidding. I'm here to case the joint for valuables and I heard they have a really nice bathroom.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'Uh, we don't... we don't discuss the special gym.'
jokes.setup: Shirley has just revealed Pierce has a 'special gym with swings and saddles' in his wine cellar
jokes.punchline: Pierce's reflexive embarrassment and stammered deflection confirms the worst and adds a beat of cringe
jokes.explanation: A quick beat that extends joke 7. Economical and character-true. The stammer is a small performance note written into the dialogue.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I got you a present!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Oh, thanks Chang. What is it?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: It's a photo from when you were younger. I thought you'd want to remember what you looked like before you got old.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm not that old, Chang.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: That's what I said. But the photo disagrees with you.

jokes.text: PA announcer: 'Oh, nice job, Manuel. And good news. There's still plenty of room in my P.A. Announcements class. Just ten bucks an hour.'
jokes.setup: The PA announcement has just ended with the announcer complimenting his assistant
jokes.punchline: The PA announcer uses the PA system to advertise his own class on making PA announcements — a perfect recursive loop
jokes.explanation: Smart meta-gag. The PA announcer using his own platform to sell a class about using his platform is a tidy recursive joke. It's also a Greendale-appropriate hustle — monetizing your institutional access.

jokes.text: Pierce reveals he's taking wine class too; Jeff's silent reaction upon seeing Pierce in the room
jokes.setup: Jeff smugly announced he was taking wine tasting to escape the group and drink in peace
jokes.punchline: Pierce shows up — his worst nightmare — and Jeff's silent take to camera/audience registers the defeat
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom beat — the character who tried to escape their group getting caught. Functional but predictable. Joel McHale's silent reaction is where the joke lives.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I'd like to see her... assets.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Hey, that's not cool. Although, I have to admit, I'm influenced by your sexism, so I kind of want to see them too.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'Got drunk ladies, fancy bathrooms, and a room full of free coats.'
jokes.setup: Pierce explains why he signed up for wine tasting
jokes.punchline: His reasons are entirely practical and predatory — no interest in wine whatsoever — culminating in 'free coats' as the third, escalating absurdity
jokes.explanation: Very Pierce. The list escalates from predatory (drunk ladies) to mundane luxury (fancy bathrooms) to genuinely inexplicable petty theft (free coats). The third item does the work — it's the least logical and most specific, which makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I'm like a fine wine, Chang. I get better with age. You're more like a cheap beer—you peak early and then it's all downhill from there.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: At least I haven't turned to vinegar yet.

jokes.text: Pierce gives Jeff an old photo: 'From before your chin dimple filled in.'
jokes.setup: Pierce says he brought Jeff a present
jokes.punchline: The 'present' is a photo that highlights a physical flaw the recipient presumably didn't want documented
jokes.explanation: Light Pierce-teasing-Jeff joke. The specificity of 'chin dimple filled in' saves it from being generic — it's a weird, specific, oddly medical-sounding insult.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'Who is the dumpling with the nice Asian pair?' — first time sexism has made someone hungry
jokes.setup: An attractive Asian woman enters the wine tasting class
jokes.punchline: Pierce's racist/sexist objectification is so confusingly mixed (food metaphor + body objectification) that Jeff's reaction — 'that's the first time sexism has made me hungry' — reframes it as comic absurdity
jokes.explanation: Jeff's response is the actual joke — it acknowledges Pierce's racism/sexism while reframing it in a way that critiques without preaching. The 'made me hungry' construction is clever and gives Jeff the superior position. Pierce's line alone would be just offensive; Jeff's reframe makes it work comedically.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, I was going to break up with her anyway. I'm seeing someone else.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'I fear I may have to let her see me nude.'
jokes.setup: Pierce is attracted to the woman and signals his intentions
jokes.punchline: He frames nudity as an obligation or inevitable next step, as if it's a burden he must shoulder — completely reversing the expected direction of desire
jokes.explanation: Classic Pierce delusion joke. By framing nudity as something he 'fears he may have to' do — as if it's a gift she's lucky to receive — it inverts desire into obligation. The phrasing 'I fear I may have to' is doing all the comedic work.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I'm gonna call myself... The Magnificent Thunderfoot!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Your real name is Troy Barnes.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I know! But The Magnificent Thunderfoot sounds way cooler!

jokes.text: Jeff says Pierce should let the wine 'breathe.' Pierce: 'I think those are wrinkles.'
jokes.setup: Jeff uses wine terminology ('let that breathe') while making a comment about Pierce's older skin
jokes.punchline: Pierce mishears or misapplies it, responding as if Jeff were commenting on his appearance
jokes.explanation: Quick bit of wordplay around wine vocabulary applied to Pierce's body. Light and fast — works as a transition joke rather than a standout.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Actually, you know what? I've been thinking about this and I really think—

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: But you didn't even—

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: "What's so funny? / Well, why would a woman want a Plymouth on cinder blocks when she could have a Testarossa, 500 horsepower with a six-speed stick? / 'Cause my stick is ribbed for her pleasure. / I think those are wrinkles."
jokes.setup: Pierce and Jeff are competing over Wu Mei; Jeff makes a car metaphor implying he's the superior option
jokes.punchline: Pierce counters with a crude sexual boast; Troy deflates it by suggesting what Pierce thinks is a ribbed stick is just age-related wrinkles
jokes.explanation: Three-beat exchange with a good structure: Jeff's smug metaphor, Pierce's crass one-upmanship, Troy's brutal deflationary punchline. Troy's line ('I think those are wrinkles') is the best part — grounding Pierce's delusion in sad physical reality. The car metaphor is a bit of a cliché setup.

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.line: Alright everyone, let's form a trust circle.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.line: A trust circle? What's that?

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.line: It's just a circle! A regular circle! Why does everyone always assume there's some deeper meaning?

jokes.text: Wu Mei introduces herself. Jeff gives a smooth line; Wu Mei: 'Not interested. Please take weird haircut, stupid grin, and go sniff another dog's ass.'
jokes.setup: Jeff deploys his standard confident charm on a beautiful woman in the wine class
jokes.punchline: She shuts him down with a spectacularly specific and vivid insult — 'go sniff another dog's ass' — completely demolishing his self-image
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best single-line deliveries. The specificity of the insult ('weird haircut, stupid grin') shows she's already catalogued his flaws; 'go sniff another dog's ass' is vivid, unexpected, and characterizes her as formidable in one line. It also destabilizes Jeff's whole arc — he's not used to this.

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.line: That's a beautiful childhood memory. Where was this playground?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Well, it was right behind my house.

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.line: And how old were you?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Seven.

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.line: That's wonderful. Thank you for sharing that with us.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Yeah, actually, that was today. I'm twenty-three.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'Hmm hmm, the red dragon ordered a number 37 with a side of pork-fried snap.'
jokes.setup: Wu Mei has firmly rejected Jeff; Pierce comments from the sideline
jokes.punchline: Pierce's response conflates the woman with a Chinese takeout order — his racism expressed as casual food-menu commentary
jokes.explanation: Cringe joke that works mainly through Pierce-character consistency rather than wit. The joke is his obliviousness, not the content. 'Pork-fried snap' is a made-up phrase that doesn't quite pay off, making it feel incomplete.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm trying to access a painful high school memory about being the football captain.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: The painful part isn't that I was popular and arrogant. The painful part is that I had to wake up at 5 AM for conditioning, and nobody told me I could just... not go.

jokes.text: Pierce, having watched Wu Mei reject Jeff: 'When you get up close, she's very homely.'
jokes.setup: Wu Mei is objectively attractive and has just humiliated Jeff in front of Pierce
jokes.punchline: Pierce — who clearly still finds her attractive — saves face by suddenly declaring her 'very homely,' a transparent lie that only makes him look worse
jokes.explanation: Economical and sharp. The punchline is delivered as a talking-head-style aside, but functions as pure delusional self-defense. The gap between obvious reality and Pierce's pronouncement is the joke. 'Very' doing ironic heavy lifting.

jokes.text: Troy: 'I can't wait till we choose stage names. Which do you think is better: Trevor St. McGoodbody or David?'
jokes.setup: Troy is excitedly preparing for the acting class, anticipating what it involves
jokes.punchline: His idea of acting involves an absurd stage name — 'Trevor St. McGoodbody' — presented alongside the completely mundane 'David' as if they're equally reasonable options
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Troy joke. 'Trevor St. McGoodbody' is a perfect name — it sounds like it was invented by a child who'd seen exactly three soap operas — and presenting 'David' as the sober alternative reveals Troy has no idea what a stage name is. The juxtaposition is the entire joke. Highly quotable and deeply character-specific.

jokes.text: Acting professor: 'Form a trust circle around me and sit on the floor.' Troy: 'A trust circle?' Professor: 'It's just a circle. It's a circle. Sit down.'
jokes.setup: The acting professor announces a 'trust circle' with what sounds like spiritual gravity
jokes.punchline: He immediately deflates his own affectation — 'It's just a circle' — the therapeutic language is revealed as empty jargon he doesn't even believe in
jokes.explanation: Smart deflation joke. The professor uses pompous theatrical language and then immediately strips it of meaning in one breath. The repetition 'It's just a circle. It's a circle.' suggests mild irritation, which makes him funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Professor
dialogue.line: Who was the boss?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Bruce Springsteen.

dialogue.speaker: Professor
dialogue.line: Class dismissed.

jokes.text: Acting professor: 'Acting is revealing, expression. When we release pain, we become visible to each other, and that is an actor's job. That and, you know, pretending to be other people.'
jokes.setup: The professor builds up an elaborate philosophical definition of acting
jokes.punchline: He punctures his own pretension by acknowledging the obvious — 'and, you know, pretending to be other people' — as if that's a minor afterthought
jokes.explanation: Good deflation joke with a slight variation on the classic 'hot air balloon deflate' structure. The delivery rhythm matters — the 'and, you know' is a perfect pause before the mundane clarification.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Pierce just completely butchered the pronunciation of 'Châteauneuf-du-Pape' and then made some offensive joke about the name that had nothing to do with French wine regions.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: What? I was just saying what I saw! 'New Pope' — I thought the Catholic Church was getting involved in the wine business!

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: It's CHÂTEAUNEUF-DU-PAPE, Pierce. It means 'new castle of the Pope' in French. There's nothing remotely amusing about your interpretation.

jokes.text: Acting professor asks for a deep and painful childhood memory. Troy launches into: 'I'm on the playground. Stop taunting me! I just want to go on the swings!' / Professor: 'Good. Early childhood is a treasure trove of pain.' / Troy: 'That happened this morning.'
jokes.setup: The professor invites the class to access deep childhood trauma; Troy begins what sounds like an earnest early childhood memory
jokes.punchline: 'That happened this morning' — Troy is not recalling childhood; he was literally bullied off swings today, revealing an adult-child dynamic that is both sad and hilarious
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The setup is perfectly misleading — the spare dialogue ('Stop taunting me! I just want to go on the swings!') reads as childhood trauma. The professor's earnest validation elevates the deception. Then 'That happened this morning' demolishes both the moment and our assumptions about Troy's development in four words. It's structurally flawless, deeply character-specific (only Troy), and devastating in its economy. The joke works on two levels: the swing incident IS genuinely sad, which makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: We're getting married.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Not immediately or anything. She's still got a husband.

jokes.text: Professor asks Jeff to share a painful memory. Jeff: 'I was captain of my high school football team.' Long pause. 'It was very hard being popular.'
jokes.setup: Acting professor pushes Jeff to access deep pain; the class leans in expectantly
jokes.punchline: Jeff's 'painful memory' is being popular and successful — his fundamental inability to access vulnerability manifests as actual comedy gold
jokes.explanation: Excellent Jeff character joke. The long beat between the football captain setup and 'It was very hard being popular' is crucial — the pause makes the audience lean in, then the punchline reveals that Jeff genuinely thinks this is a trauma worth sharing. It's a character joke that also advances his arc: Jeff's emotional inaccessibility is both his flaw and his comedy engine.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Stranger things have happened.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: No, they haven't.

jokes.text: [Beat — silent reaction from the acting class after Jeff's 'painful memory' about being popular]
jokes.setup: Jeff delivers his 'painful memory' of being popular
jokes.punchline: The implied silence/dismissal — professor moves on without comment: 'Okay, great. Next person.' — the lack of engagement is the punchline
jokes.explanation: 'Okay, great. Next person.' is a perfect dismissal that functions as both polite and devastating. The professor's complete non-engagement with Jeff's brag-as-pain is funny precisely because she doesn't even bother to unpack it. Visual beat inferred from the transcript's abrupt move-on.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I went up to her and said, 'Are you a Chinese takeout menu? Because I want to fold you in half and put you in my pocket.'

jokes.text: A student shares feeling invisible and ignored; mid-sentence, another student blurts: 'My uncle put his finger in my no-no!'
jokes.setup: A quiet student begins a genuinely relatable confession about feeling invisible — the class is finally having an authentic moment
jokes.punchline: Pierce (or another student) explosively interrupts with an abuse disclosure phrased in juvenile language ('no-no'), completely hijacking the moment
jokes.explanation: Very effective escalation joke. The invisible student's setup is a classic straight-man moment designed to be interrupted; the interruption is perfectly pitched — a TMI disclosure in childlike language. 'No-no' as the euphemism is the key comedic choice, infantilizing the content to make it both more absurd and more cringe. This joke has legs — it sets up the Troy-Britta subplot.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: For extremely dangerous fireworks

jokes.text: Professor Sheffield begins: 'Welcome to a Critical Analysis of Who's the Boss? I am Professor Peter Sheffield, and I'd like to begin with a simple question... [long pause] ...Who was the boss?'
jokes.setup: An academic professor introduces an entire course dedicated to analyzing Who's the Boss?
jokes.punchline: The profound, weighted opening question — delivered with Socratic gravitas after a dramatic pause — is simply the show's title
jokes.explanation: Smart comedy of academic self-importance. The extended buildup — formal introduction, 'simple question,' dramatic pause — frames the question as philosophical; then the question is literally just the TV show's title. The gap between the gravity of the delivery and the triviality of the content is the entire joke. Perfectly constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: We'll be together forever.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Well, as long as you don't gain more than fifteen pounds.

jokes.text: "Yes. / Angela. / Oh, well! Class dismissed!"
jokes.setup: Sheffield poses his life's central question with great gravitas
jokes.punchline: Abed immediately and confidently answers 'Angela,' causing Sheffield to sarcastically declare class dismissed — his life's work apparently solved in five seconds
jokes.explanation: Perfect Abed joke that also captures Sheffield's pathology instantly. Abed's confident 'Angela' is both probably correct (the audience of Who's the Boss? largely agrees) and devastating to a man who has staked his career on it being an open question. Sheffield's sarcastic 'Class dismissed!' is wounded and funny — delivered by someone whose worst nightmare is having a simple answer. The economy is excellent; the character integration for both Abed and Sheffield is high.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I've had more romantic encounters than you've had study sessions.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I once made a woman climax just by describing my bone structure.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Another time, I seduced a girl with a single wink. She didn't even know what hit her.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm basically a sexual god among mortals.

jokes.text: "Yes. / Angela. / Oh, well! Class dismissed!"
jokes.setup: Sheffield asks 'Who was the boss?' expecting to unpack deep academic theory; Abed simply answers 'Angela'
jokes.punchline: Sheffield's 'Oh, well! Class dismissed!' — delivered as a joke about how Abed has just solved the entire course in one word, then immediately walking it back ('No, calm down') — sets up the ongoing conflict while being funny in its pure absurdist logic
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest academic-satire jokes. Abed cutting through Sheffield's entire course framework in one word triggers a momentary panic-class-dismissal. 'Oh, well! Class dismissed!' is a perfect absurdist response — Sheffield's entire life's work punctured by a student who hasn't even opened the book. This works because Abed's literalism vs. the Professor's obfuscation is a great character dynamic. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Jeff's been working really hard. I'm worried he's getting worked up.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Troy, you need to stop enabling his behavior. He's using work as a defense mechanism to avoid processing his deep-seated abandonment issues.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: He's just studying for a test.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Exactly. Classic avoidance pattern.

jokes.text: Pierce refused to drink Pinot Noir because he thought it meant 'black penis' in French.
jokes.setup: Shirley explains why wine tasting with Pierce is difficult
jokes.punchline: Pierce's faux-French pronunciation paranoia leads him to refuse an entire wine varietal based on a completely wrong translation
jokes.explanation: 'Pinot' does sound vaguely like a certain word to an untrained ear, and 'noir' means black — so Pierce's racist anxiety has a twisted logic to it. It's a character joke that reveals his racism through faux-prudishness rather than outright slurs, which is more interesting. Well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Britta's attracted to broken things because she's broken. It's a defense mechanism. She'll date you, realize you're not actually damaged, and leave you for someone with real problems. It's why she dates so much.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I'm standing right here.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I know. This is part of why you'll never change.

jokes.text: Pierce arrives at the study group table with Wu Mei: 'Everybody, this is Wu Mei, and we're getting married! But it's not gonna be today.'
jokes.setup: Pierce makes a dramatic engagement announcement
jokes.punchline: The clarification — 'but it's not gonna be today' — is the topper that makes no sense as reassurance. As if the concern was timing, not the relationship itself.
jokes.explanation: 'But it's not gonna be today' is a great topper — the unnecessary qualifier suggests Pierce anticipated the wrong objection entirely. It also works as a beat of pure comic timing, letting the announcement breathe before deflating.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Actually, it wasn't just one time. There were multiple incidents. He used to make me sing show tunes while he... while he did things.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Troy.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: And the worst part? He had really good taste in musicals. So now whenever I hear 'Defying Gravity,' I just...

jokes.text: "He wouldn't miss a chance to pop in and say something offensive. / [Pierce enters with Wu Mei] / Everybody, this is Wu Mei, and we're getting married! But it's not gonna be today."
jokes.setup: Jeff predicts Pierce will show up and say something offensive
jokes.punchline: Pierce shows up — not with something offensive but with the announcement he's getting married. The 'but it's not gonna be today' kicker is a deadpan afterthought that makes the announcement more absurd.
jokes.explanation: Good subversion — the prediction of something offensive is fulfilled by something arguably worse (an engagement announcement). The 'but it's not gonna be today' kicker is a perfectly dry absurdist addition. The entry timing is well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: My heart is a football, and it just got intercepted by the blitz of life.

jokes.text: 'Well, stranger things have happened.' 'No. No, they haven't.'
jokes.setup: Pierce tries to minimize how unexpected his engagement announcement is
jokes.punchline: Shirley's flat, immediate denial — with no qualification or softening
jokes.explanation: Economy joke. 'No. No, they haven't.' is maximally direct — no metaphor, no hedging. The double 'No' and the period-then-restatement structure makes it funnier than a single denial. Shirley playing straight woman here is exactly right.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So what do you know about Pierce?

dialogue.speaker: Wu Mei
dialogue.line: Oh, Pierce? He's a young, athletic guy. Very into social media. Always talking about his cryptocurrency portfolio. Super trendy fashion sense. Really into TikTok dances.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: ...Are you describing Pierce Hawthorne?

dialogue.speaker: Wu Mei
dialogue.line: Yes. Why?

jokes.text: Pierce: 'I mentioned that her breasts were larger than most Asian women, and we just got to talking.'
jokes.setup: Pierce explains how he and Wu Mei fell for each other
jokes.punchline: His opening line to her was an objectifying racial comparison — and apparently it worked as a conversation starter
jokes.explanation: Classic Pierce-oblivious cringe. The specificity of the racial comparison is what makes it his voice specifically. The 'and we just got to talking' as if this is a perfectly reasonable ice-breaker is the comedic payoff. Not the episode's sharpest but lands.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: That's why they call me Irony-Free Annie.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, the other stuff they call you is way worse.

jokes.text: Pierce explains the China connection: 'It's the only place to get fireworks that are too dangerous for Mexico.'
jokes.setup: Pierce explains why he's been to China many times
jokes.punchline: He goes to China for fireworks too dangerous for Mexico — an escalating specificity joke about danger thresholds
jokes.explanation: Genuinely clever joke. The hierarchical danger structure (too dangerous for Mexico, therefore must source from China) has a weird internal logic that makes it funnier. It's also a great worldbuilding beat for Pierce: he is the kind of person who seeks out fireworks too dangerous for an entire country.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: My mind is open.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: But not so open that I don't know you're acting like Angela from Who's the Boss?.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'I go to visit my factory. Hawthorne Wipes are the number one moist towelette in Asia.'
jokes.setup: Pierce continues to explain his China connection
jokes.punchline: The pivot to moist towelette manufacturing — presented with genuine corporate pride — is an absurd tonal shift from dangerous fireworks
jokes.explanation: Setup joke for the later Hawthorne Wipes / Red Dragon Wipes corporate espionage reveal. As a standalone it's modest — the comedy is mainly in 'moist towelette' as a product to be proud of.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Cool. Cool cool cool cool cool cool cool.

jokes.text: "Or at least until she gets heavy."
jokes.setup: Pierce says he and Wu Mei are meant to be together forever
jokes.punchline: He immediately qualifies it: 'Or at least until she gets heavy' — revealing the conditional nature of his devotion
jokes.explanation: Classic Pierce: undercuts his own romantic gesture with an appearance-based caveat. The casualness of delivery is the joke — he isn't trying to be funny or cruel, he's just stating his terms. 'Gets heavy' is a slightly unusual phrasing that makes it funnier than 'gains weight' would be. Character-consistent but not an outlier for Pierce material.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I'm touched you guys threw me an engagement party.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, we were threatened.

jokes.text: Annie: 'Plan an engagement party?' Jeff: 'Are you out of your mind?! This is a scam. She's after him for his money or a green card.'
jokes.setup: The group reacts to Pierce's engagement announcement
jokes.punchline: Jeff's immediate cynicism is accurate but delivered with such disproportionate outrage that it becomes comedy — especially ironic given that Jeff is usually the last one to care about anyone
jokes.explanation: Functional plot/character beat. Jeff's cynicism is consistent but not particularly well-crafted here — the comedy comes more from the situation than the writing.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You're like the Oprah of this place.

dialogue.speaker: Wu Mei
dialogue.line: I'm nothing like Oprah.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Well, you're both... you're both very successful and influential women.

dialogue.speaker: Wu Mei
dialogue.line: That's literally all we have in common.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Exactly! And you're both... not white.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'I had a three-way in a hot air balloon.'
jokes.setup: Annie accuses Jeff of not understanding romance
jokes.punchline: Jeff's rebuttal is a casually dropped sexual adventure as proof of romantic credentials
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy joke. Five words, complete image, complete character. Jeff's conception of romance as extreme sexual adventure (with witnesses, at altitude) is both funny and deeply revealing. The specificity of 'hot air balloon' — not even a sexy location, just an extreme one — is what makes it land.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, and like a baboon, you throw your feces at people when they get too close.

jokes.text: Troy explains he made up the uncle story to attract Britta: 'Britta's attracted to men in pain. It helps her pretend to be mentally healthy.'
jokes.setup: Troy confides that his abuse story was fabricated; Abed explains his reasoning
jokes.punchline: Abed's clinical diagnosis of Britta's psychology — 'it helps her pretend to be mentally healthy' — is both savage and accurate
jokes.explanation: Very sharp Abed line. His ability to analyze others' psychology without affect or judgment is one of his defining comedic traits, and 'it helps her pretend to be mentally healthy' is a precise and devastating character insight delivered in one subordinate clause. High character integration — no other character on this show could deliver this line.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: You see, I've prepared a backup meal in case they refuse to serve me.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: It's not paranoia if it's happened before. I've got lo mein in my pocket, a thermos of soup in my jacket, and emergency dumplings in my socks.

jokes.text: Abed: 'Troy? Nothing good can come of this.' Troy: 'Yeah. I'll have to think really hard about how to defuse the situation.' Immediately: 'No, uncle Lucius! I don't want to play in the laundry room! My emotions!'
jokes.setup: Troy acknowledges the problem with his lie and says he'll think hard about how to fix it
jokes.punchline: He immediately escalates the lie instead — adding 'uncle Lucius' and a specific location, then performing a full emotional breakdown
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation joke. The structure is perfect: verbal acknowledgment of the problem, faux-deliberation, then immediate and opposite action. 'Uncle Lucius' is a great comedy name, and 'I don't want to play in the laundry room!' is specific enough to suggest a real story. 'My emotions!' as a finale is a great performance-within-performance beat.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: In Chinese culture, the family name comes first, then the given name. It's a sign of respect for your ancestors.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Of course, back in the day, they'd name their kids things like 'Cow Tooth' and 'Broken Stick.' So maybe the order doesn't matter as much as we think.

jokes.text: Acting professor dismisses class: 'Actors dismissed.' Then: 'For homework, drink a glass of cognac in a bathtub.'
jokes.setup: The acting class is dismissed
jokes.punchline: The homework assignment is to drink cognac in a bathtub — a lifestyle prescription with no apparent pedagogical purpose
jokes.explanation: Good absurdist professor joke. The specificity of cognac-in-bathtub as homework reveals this professor assigns self-indulgent activities as 'actor preparation' — it's a type. The delivery matters: 'Actors dismissed' establishes faux-grandeur, then the absurd assignment punctures it.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Pierce, that's not what that means.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Well, I'm going to keep saying it anyway because I like the way it sounds.

jokes.text: Britta: 'Troy, I feel like I'm seeing a whole different side of you. There's just so much darkness.' Troy (performing): 'And my soul is darkening, and my heart is mad at my kidneys, and... [kisses her]'
jokes.setup: Britta is moved by Troy's (fabricated) emotional vulnerability
jokes.punchline: Troy's performed anguish escalates to anatomically confused organ-blaming ('my heart is mad at my kidneys'), then uses the momentum to kiss her — confirming the manipulation worked
jokes.explanation: 'My heart is mad at my kidneys' is a great absurdist line — the organ-blaming reveals Troy doesn't quite know what emotional pain sounds like, so he invents organ-on-organ conflict. The kiss confirms the whole scheme worked, which pays off the deception setup.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Pierce, you really need to be more sensitive about the language you use.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: What? I'm cool with it.

jokes.text: Jeff tries to offer Wu Mei a friendly second meeting; she immediately counters his immigration/legal offers with dual citizenship, family lawyers, and a family fortune.
jokes.setup: Jeff uses his lawyer credentials to suggest he can help with immigration and prenup issues — implying Wu Mei needs his resources
jokes.punchline: She systematically refutes every supposed advantage Jeff had, culminating in her family fortune dwarfing Pierce's
jokes.explanation: Good reversal structure. Jeff's assumption of his own usefulness is systematically demolished. Each counter is a beat in a satisfying escalating reversal. Wu Mei's calm competence is itself the joke — she doesn't even get annoyed.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I made it all up. There was no molestation. I just wanted to see if I could get away with it.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Why isn't anyone laughing?

jokes.text: "If you need any help navigating the whole green card immigration hassle. / I am dual citizen already. / Oh. Well, if you'd like me to look at the prenup... / I assume you have one. / Yes, but my father's lawyers will take care of this. After all, we must protect our family fortune."
jokes.setup: Jeff is trying to investigate whether Wu Mei has ulterior motives by subtly offering legal services
jokes.punchline: Every angle Jeff tries is countered — she's a dual citizen (no green card needed), she has her own lawyers, and her family has a fortune to protect — completely reversing the power dynamic Jeff assumed
jokes.explanation: Good escalating reversal structure — Jeff's every probe is deflected by Wu Mei having more than he expected. The cumulative effect of Jeff's investigation failing at every turn while Wu Mei remains perfectly pleasant builds well.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wu Mei, I've uncovered your entire operation. The shell companies in the Cayman Islands, the forged credentials, the infiltration of Greendale—it's all here.

dialogue.speaker: Wu Mei
dialogue.line: You Googled me.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I... yes, but—

dialogue.speaker: Wu Mei
dialogue.line: For like twenty minutes.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Now I'm stumped.' Wu Mei: 'Excuse me?' Jeff: 'Uh, it was... that means it was very nice talking to you.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is out of angles after Wu Mei demolishes all his leverage
jokes.punchline: He mutters his defeat ('Now I'm stumped') then bizarrely pretends 'stumped' is Italian for a compliment
jokes.explanation: Decent save-face joke. Jeff's desperate improvised lie ('that's Italian for...') reveals a rare moment of Jeff not having a move. The implausibility of 'stumped' as an Italian compliment is the gap the joke lives in.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Well, I'm not afraid to admit it — I conquered that woman like a European colonizer.

jokes.text: "Hmm. / Now I'm stumped. / Excuse me? / Uh, it was... That means it was very nice talking to you."
jokes.setup: Jeff's investigation of Wu Mei has completely collapsed — she has money, citizenship, everything
jokes.punchline: He mutters 'Now I'm stumped' aloud, then has to hastily pretend it means something in Italian: 'That means it was very nice talking to you'
jokes.explanation: Good self-rescue comedy moment. Jeff accidentally reveals his genuine confusion, then tries to pass it off as Italian — a transparent save that Wu Mei clearly sees through ('if you say so'). The gap between Jeff's self-image as smooth operator and his stumbling reality is the consistent joke of this episode.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You weren't trying to help me, Jeff. You were trying to help yourself feel like a good person. And the saddest part? It almost worked.

jokes.text: Annie: 'Maybe Pierce finally found his soul mate. How can you say those things without any trace of irony?' Jeff: 'That's why they call me irony-free Annie.' Annie: 'Mm, trust me, that's not what they call you.'
jokes.setup: Annie defends Pierce sincerely; Jeff labels her 'irony-free Annie'
jokes.punchline: Annie's comeback — 'that's not what they call you' — implies a less flattering nickname without stating it, using Jeff's own rhetorical structure against him
jokes.explanation: Annie gets a rare sharp comeback against Jeff. The implication joke (without specifying the actual nickname) is smarter than spelling it out. Good character beat for Annie asserting herself.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I'm just hoping to fall for someone healthy and normal for once.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Well, I'm pretty normal.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Troy, you're afraid of ceiling fans.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Ceiling fans are a real threat!

jokes.text: Professor Sheffield shows Abed his wall of photographs with Tony Danza, Judith Light, Alyssa Milano, the Season 3 caterer, and 'Gordon Giddy-up Galligan.'
jokes.setup: Professor Sheffield tries to establish his academic credibility over Abed
jokes.punchline: His wall of credentials includes the show's caterer and a person with a ridiculous nickname — the escalating specificity revealing obsession, not scholarship
jokes.explanation: Great escalation joke. The list starts with legitimate cast (Danza, Light, Milano), pivots to the Season 3 caterer as an equal, then ends on 'Gordon Giddy-up Galligan' — a name so specific it must be a real but minor crew member. The caterer and Giddy-up are what make this a character reveal: he's not a scholar, he's a superfan.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I lied. There was no molestation. I just wanted attention.

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.line: Well, that's disappointing. I already typed up the report.

jokes.text: Abed: 'My mind is open, Professor. It's as open as the door to Mona's bedroom. It's a shame yours isn't.'
jokes.setup: Professor Sheffield tells Abed to leave for challenging his thesis
jokes.punchline: Abed uses a Who's the Boss? reference ('Mona's bedroom' — an open-door running gag from the show) to simultaneously make a point about academic openness AND flex deeper show knowledge than the professor
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Abed line. Using show-specific lore as a rhetorical device is exactly what Abed does — he weaponizes his encyclopedic TV knowledge in an argument about TV scholarship. It's character-integrated at the highest level. The move defeats Sheffield on his own turf, which is the structural elegance of the joke. Only Abed could deliver this.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I just want to be interesting.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Duncan
dialogue.line: You know what's interesting? The fact that you want to be interesting makes you interesting. But the moment you become interesting, you'll stop wanting to be interesting, which makes you uninteresting again. So the only way to stay interesting is to never achieve your goal of being interesting.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: ...I hate this class.

jokes.text: Professor Sheffield, unable to refute Abed, 'punishes' him by assigning him to teach the next class: 'Why don't you teach the next class? That way you can share your open mind with everybody.'
jokes.setup: Sheffield is intellectually cornered by Abed and needs to regain authority
jokes.punchline: His 'punishment' is actually an opportunity — he accidentally gives Abed exactly what he wants (a platform), which will backfire spectacularly
jokes.explanation: Setup-for-payoff joke. The comedy here is structural — Sheffield thinks he's punishing Abed; the audience knows Abed will absolutely kill it. The 'cool cool cool' that follows confirms Abed's delight.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: After extensive analysis of power dynamics, hierarchical structures, and interpersonal relationships within our group, I've completed my comprehensive study on who, definitively, is the boss.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: It's Britta.

jokes.text: Abed: 'Cool. Cool cool cool. Pchew.'
jokes.setup: Abed is 'punished' by being given the chance to teach the class
jokes.punchline: Abed's signature 'cool cool cool' — a signal that something has gone exactly according to his preferences — plus 'Pchew' (a gun-finger sound effect) confirms his complete satisfaction
jokes.explanation: One of Community's most iconic character tics. 'Cool cool cool' is Abed's tell for secret satisfaction, and the 'pchew' finger-gun is an irresistible punctuation mark. The quotability on this is extremely high — it's become a cultural shorthand. Very low-effort, very high-reward character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: They're doing an all-black production of Fiddler on the Roof.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: It's called Fiddler on the Roof... of Harlem.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'I couldn't be more touched that you all threw us an engagement party.' Shirley: 'You said if we didn't, you'd slash our tires.' Pierce: 'She is funny. Like Oprah.' Shirley: 'Oprah's not a comedienne.' Pierce: 'No, you are funny, and you are like Oprah.'
jokes.setup: Pierce expresses gratitude for the engagement party
jokes.punchline: Three-beat joke: (1) Shirley reveals the party was coerced by tire-slashing threat; (2) Pierce compliments her with the wrong reference; (3) When corrected, he doubles down in a way that is simultaneously more racist and more accurate
jokes.explanation: Very good three-beat structure. The first beat (tires) is a great deflation; the second (Oprah) shows Pierce defaulting to a Black celebrity comparison that's both wrong and vaguely racist; the third correction/doubling-down is the best beat — Pierce separates the two compliments and means both sincerely, which is somehow worse.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Seems like just yesterday me and Abed dined and ditched here.' [reaction shot / nostalgic pause]
jokes.setup: Jeff makes a nostalgic comment at the restaurant
jokes.punchline: The implied visual: Jeff getting sentimental about a petty crime as if it were a cherished memory
jokes.explanation: Light texture joke. Jeff's fondness for his own bad behavior as 'memories' is consistent with his character but not particularly crafted here.

jokes.text: "Seems like just yesterday me and Abed dined and ditched here."
jokes.setup: The group is at a restaurant for the engagement party
jokes.punchline: Troy casually mentions that he and Abed previously dined and ditched at this same restaurant — delivered with nostalgia, as if it's a cherished memory
jokes.explanation: Minor character note — Troy and Abed's friendship history rendered in a casual crime confession. The nostalgic delivery is funny but it's a quick gag without much payoff.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'Here, hold this.' Jeff: 'What is this?' Pierce: 'I always carry some spare apps in case the wait staff's racist.'
jokes.setup: Pierce hands Jeff something at the restaurant
jokes.punchline: He carries contingency appetizers in case of racist service — a plan that reveals more about Pierce's worldview (and his expectations of himself being targeted) than he intends
jokes.explanation: Surprisingly sharp joke. The absurdist premise (carrying backup apps for racist service situations) reveals Pierce's self-awareness is exactly one step removed from reality — he understands racism exists and that he might face it, but his solution is to carry food as a contingency rather than, say, not being racist himself. The joke works both as Pierce-character comedy and as a sly commentary on his contradictions.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'Hats off to Pierce and the hot red dragon.' Jeff: 'Why do you keep calling her that?' Pierce: 'Hong Long means red dragon. But that's her middle name.' Pierce: 'In China, they put the last name first. I mean, they're nuts over there.'
jokes.setup: Pierce uses Wu Mei's name in a seemingly offensive way; Jeff questions it
jokes.punchline: Pierce actually knows the accurate translation AND the correct cultural convention — but frames his accurate knowledge as evidence of Chinese eccentricity ('they're nuts over there'), which is itself the joke
jokes.explanation: Smart joke that sets up the later corporate espionage reveal. Pierce using 'Red Dragon' as a nickname inadvertently names the competing company. His accurate knowledge delivered with cultural dismissal is a classic Pierce paradox — he knows things but misinterprets them in self-serving ways.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'So the drinks are on me, but stick to the crappy stuff. I don't want to get corn-holed on the bar tab.' [Group reacts]
jokes.setup: Pierce makes a toast and offers to pay for drinks
jokes.punchline: He uses 'corn-holed' as a synonym for 'ripped off' — an entirely unself-conscious deployment of a vulgar double entendre
jokes.explanation: Classic Pierce oblivious-vulgarity joke. The group's reaction (and what follows) is what elevates it. The escalation into Troy's correction is funnier than the initial line.

jokes.text: "I know it seems fast, but when you find the right person, you just know it. I know that because I've found the right person seven times."
jokes.setup: Pierce makes a romantic speech about knowing when you've found the right person
jokes.punchline: He's found 'the right person' seven times — the romantic certainty is completely undermined by the number of times it has failed
jokes.explanation: One of Pierce's best lines in the episode. The structure is clean: sincere romantic wisdom immediately self-demolished by its own evidence. 'Seven times' is the perfect number — large enough to be absurd but specific enough to be sad. Pierce delivers it without any awareness that the number undermines the message. High quotability, strong economy.

jokes.text: Pierce repeating 'corn-hole, corn-hole!' after being told to stop. Annie: 'Pierce! Troy was molested!' Pierce: 'Cool.'
jokes.setup: Pierce won't stop saying 'corn-hole'; Annie tries to stop him by invoking Troy's (fake) trauma
jokes.punchline: Pierce's immediate 'Cool.' — not horror or sympathy, just casual acknowledgment — is a perfect Pierce response that reveals his complete emotional disconnect
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy joke. 'Cool.' as a response to a molestation disclosure is devastating in its brevity — it reveals Pierce has zero social calibration while also being wildly inappropriate in a way that's undeniably funny. The single-word response does more character work than a paragraph could. Also functions as a great misdirection: Annie's serious invocation of Troy's trauma is immediately deflated.

jokes.text: Troy: 'Troy, do you need me to recommend a support group?' Troy: 'Hey, he's not a victim. You're a survivor.'
jokes.setup: The group rallies around Troy's fabricated abuse story with sincere support
jokes.punchline: The sincerity of support for a made-up story is itself the cringe joke; the distinction between 'victim' and 'survivor' applied to a lie escalates the discomfort
jokes.explanation: Good cringe beat. The mismatch between sincere support and fictional trauma creates the discomfort. The survivor/victim distinction being applied with earnestness to a lie is a sharp detail.

jokes.text: Troy: 'Yeah, about that... I wasn't so much molested as much as I made it up.' Then: 'We're gonna laugh so hard about this later.'
jokes.setup: The group has just surrounded Troy with emotional support for his abuse story
jokes.punchline: Troy casually confesses the fabrication with 'made it up,' then tries to skip ahead to the future laughing phase with 'we're gonna laugh so hard about this later'
jokes.explanation: Excellent payoff to the Troy subplot. 'We're gonna laugh so hard about this later' is a perfect deflection — Troy immediately tries to time-skip to the phase where everyone forgives him, which is both cowardly and very Troy. The preemptive laugh appeal as a conflict resolution tool is sharp and quotable.

jokes.text: Jeff's toast: 'Wu Mei Hong Long, better known as Mei Hong Long Wu, is not only not a Greendale student — she works for Red Dragon Wipes, the number two wipe in Asia, currently attempting a takeover of Hawthorne Wipes.'
jokes.setup: Jeff stands to propose a toast at the engagement party — the group expects a toast
jokes.punchline: Instead he delivers a full corporate espionage revelation using the toast format, including 'the number two wipe in Asia' as a straight-faced dramatic revelation
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to multiple setups. 'The number two wipe in Asia' delivered with toast-solemnity is funny, and the corporate espionage reveal using a party toast structure is a good situational joke. The callback to Pierce's 'red dragon' nickname paying off as the competitor's actual brand name is satisfying.

jokes.text: Jeff: '...and to me for being attractive enough to get a girl like her under normal circumstances.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is making a toast about heroically exposing a corporate spy
jokes.punchline: He adds a self-congratulatory coda about his own attractiveness — inserting ego into what was briefly a selfless act
jokes.explanation: Perfect Jeff character beat. The reveal is dramatic and heroic, then he pivots immediately to 'and to me for being hot enough to attract her.' The narcissism returning precisely when it's least appropriate is on-brand and well-timed.

jokes.text: Wu Mei: 'Very impressive, Veronica Mars. You learned how to use Google.' Jeff: 'And you learned to fight your physical desire for me.' Wu Mei: 'Oh, stick it. You suck.'
jokes.setup: Jeff reveals Wu Mei's spy status; she responds
jokes.punchline: Wu Mei compares Jeff to Veronica Mars as a diminutive — a teenager detective — and the exchange becomes a rapid-fire volley of insults ending with the blunt 'Oh, stick it. You suck.'
jokes.explanation: Good banter. 'Veronica Mars' as an insult (calling out that his investigation was just Googling) is clever. Jeff's counter — 'you learned to fight your physical desire for me' — reasserts his ego after a defeat. 'Oh, stick it. You suck.' is a satisfying blunt shutdown.

jokes.text: Pierce pulls out a 'record scratch app' on his phone to dramatically pause the moment.
jokes.setup: The engagement party has just erupted in chaos after Jeff's reveal
jokes.punchline: Pierce deploys a literal record-scratch sound effect app to pause the drama — using his phone to perform a TV cliché in real life
jokes.explanation: Smart meta-joke. The record scratch is a TV/film convention for freezing a dramatic moment; Pierce having an actual app for this collapses the fictional device into diegetic reality. It's also slightly Pierce-specific — of course he has a record scratch app. The gap between intended gravitas and execution is funny.

jokes.text: "Record scratch app." [Troy produces a phone that plays a record scratch sound effect]
jokes.setup: The engagement party has descended into chaos after the corporate spy reveal
jokes.punchline: Troy has a 'record scratch app' on his phone and deploys it to freeze the moment — the gag is both a meta-reference to narrative convention AND reveals that Troy owns and uses this app
jokes.explanation: One of the more inventive meta-jokes in the episode. The record scratch is a cinematic/narrative device — Troy having it as a literal phone app that he deploys in real life is both a meta-commentary on TV conventions AND perfectly Troy (of course he has this app). The reveal that he uses it in social situations is delightful. Highly quotable and rewatchable.

jokes.text: 'Where'd everybody go?' / 'Most people went home. The rest went with Chang to your place to have a ketchup fight.' Pierce: 'Oh jeez, I better get back there before he starts playing monkey drop. Don't ask.'
jokes.setup: Pierce emerges from his dramatic pause to find the room empty
jokes.punchline: The explanation for where people went includes a ketchup fight, and Pierce's concern about 'monkey drop' (never defined, never explained) is a perfect absurdist non-sequitur
jokes.explanation: 'Monkey drop. Don't ask.' is a great Community joke type: the implied unseen absurdity that is never explained. The audience's imagination fills in something worse than anything the writers could show. The ketchup fight sets up the gag, but 'monkey drop' is the actual punchline.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'I was just using her to get her company in the sack. People use each other, Jeff. It doesn't mean there aren't good feelings that go along with it.' Then: 'I liked her. She was busty.'
jokes.setup: Pierce makes a surprisingly mature point about mutual use in relationships — 'people use each other'
jokes.punchline: The philosophical build is punctured by 'I liked her. She was busty.' — his summarizing emotion is entirely physical
jokes.explanation: Good Pierce moment that walks the line between pathos and comedy. 'People use each other' almost works as genuine wisdom before 'She was busty' completely deflates it. The deflation is the joke, but the genuine feeling underneath makes it land as more than just crass.

jokes.text: Britta: 'Troy, kissing you was a mistake. It will never happen again.' Troy: 'Good.'
jokes.setup: Britta delivers a serious, slightly harsh rejection to Troy
jokes.punchline: Troy's 'Good.' — relief rather than disappointment — completely subverts the expected emotional beat
jokes.explanation: Perfect subversion. Britta sets up an uncomfortable rejection scene; Troy's one-word relief response (a) ends the scene efficiently and (b) reveals he never actually wanted her — it was pure strategic manipulation. The economy is exceptional: 'Good.' does everything.

jokes.text: Britta explains her ex-boyfriend Pablo, 'huffed up on paint thinners,' who accused her of only being attracted to damaged men — 'it was hard to understand him though, he was pretty huffed up on paint thinners.'
jokes.setup: Britta is sharing a moment of self-reflection prompted by Troy, and references an ex who pointed out her pattern
jokes.punchline: The ex was 'huffed up on paint thinners' — his testimony about her damage-attraction pattern is undermined by his method of delivery, while simultaneously confirming the pattern (she dated a paint thinner huffer)
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best Britta jokes. The setup (he accused her of liking damaged men) is immediately evidence-proven by the punchline (she dated a paint thinner addict). The structure is self-eating: citing the testimony of a huffer as a credible character witness while unknowingly proving his point is elegant and very Britta. High originality — the specific detail of 'paint thinner' rather than a generic drug elevates it.

jokes.text: Troy: 'Someone who, other than his irrational fear of automatic toilets, is normal.'
jokes.setup: Troy is describing what a healthy romantic partner for Britta might look like
jokes.punchline: His parenthetical self-description ('other than his irrational fear of automatic toilets') gives himself away as the candidate — and the specific fear is both absurd and very Troy
jokes.explanation: Excellent Troy character joke. The fear of automatic toilets is specific, irrational, and completely believable for Troy — suggesting a whole offscreen history of incidents. His casual disclosure of this in a parenthetical while nominally describing someone else makes it funnier. The 'is normal' conclusion after admitting a weird phobia is a good structural beat.

jokes.text: Acting class: Troy confesses his uncle story was fabricated. 'I want to be interesting. I want to fit in with you guys. I want to be able to be an actor.'
jokes.setup: Troy confesses he has no real painful experience to share
jokes.punchline: His reason for fabricating trauma is that he wants to 'fit in' — a genuinely sad and funny admission about the currency of pain in therapeutic/artistic spaces
jokes.explanation: Genuine-pathos-meets-comedy moment. The desire to fake trauma to fit into an artistic community is a sharp satirical point about performative vulnerability culture, delivered through Troy without being preachy. Functions more as emotional resolution than pure comedy.

jokes.text: "I know. I'm bummed about it, too." [Acting Professor's response to Troy's uncle confession]
jokes.setup: Troy confesses his uncle story was fake
jokes.punchline: The professor's response is 'I'm bummed about it, too' — she's mourning the loss of dramatic material, not comforting a victim
jokes.explanation: Perfect. 'I'm bummed about it, too' is exactly what a certain kind of acting teacher would say — she's sad she lost her best student material, not sympathetic to the deception. It instantly characterizes her entire philosophy (pain as raw material) in five words. High economy.

jokes.text: Acting professor: 'The pain of not having enough pain is still pain, young man. That may seem like an easy resolution, but... we're not writers. We're actors. Story doesn't matter here. All that matters is our time in the spotlight.'
jokes.setup: Troy confesses he has no real pain and was faking it
jokes.punchline: The professor validates him with a meaningless tautology ('the pain of not having enough pain is still pain') then reveals acting class is not actually about truth but about spotlight — undercutting all the earlier pretension about pain and visibility
jokes.explanation: Very good satirical moment. 'The pain of not having enough pain is still pain' is a perfectly constructed therapeutic non-sense tautology — you can hear this in real acting classes. The reveal that 'story doesn't matter, only the spotlight' inverts everything the professor spent the episode claiming. It's character-consistent and thematically resonant.

jokes.text: Abed teaching the Who's the Boss? class, working through eleven analytical criteria, culminating in a formal verdict: 'The empirically provable answer to the question who's the boss is... Angela Bauer.'
jokes.setup: Abed has been assigned to teach the class and present his thesis
jokes.punchline: After elaborate academic scaffolding and 'eleven possible fields' of analysis, the conclusion is exactly what he said in the first five minutes of class — it's Angela
jokes.explanation: Perfect episodic callback payoff. The joke is structural: Abed was right at minute one, and the entire course's academic apparatus leads back to the same answer. Sheffield's whole life's work is validated and invalidated simultaneously. The formal 'empirically provable' framing for a TV show analysis is Abed's character in pure form.

jokes.text: "Are you still thinking about studying acting? / I'm auditioning for Professor Garrity's all-black production of Fiddler on the Roof. / It's called Fiddla Please."
jokes.setup: Shirley asks about Troy's acting plans after the class drama
jokes.punchline: 'Fiddla Please' as the title of the all-Black Fiddler on the Roof — a punny, culturally specific rebranding that works on multiple levels
jokes.explanation: 'Fiddla Please' is a genuinely clever joke. It's a pun (Fiddler → Fiddla), a cultural reclamation gag, and an AAVE/slang subversion ('please' as dismissive/'on the roof' dropped), all in two words. The setup 'all-black production of Fiddler on the Roof' earns the rename. High quotability — the kind of joke people repeat. Strong originality relative to the episode's other jokes.

jokes.text: Annie tells Jeff she's set Pierce and Wu Mei up on a real date: 'You're both rude, you're both deceitful and racist, and you both come from moist wipe dynasties.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is surprised to find Wu Mei at their hangout spot and that Annie invited her
jokes.punchline: Annie's matchmaking rationale is entirely negative qualities — their compatibility rests on shared rudeness, deceit, racism, and industrial moist wipe empires
jokes.explanation: Great Annie character moment. Her earnest matchmaking based entirely on shared flaws is both logical (by Community logic) and funny. 'Moist wipe dynasties' as a romantic compatibility metric is perfect — the specificity elevates the whole list.

jokes.text: "I guess we could go out to one dinner. / You're paying. / You're dressing slutty."
jokes.setup: Pierce and Wu Mei agree to a real date
jokes.punchline: Their instant negotiation — Pierce demands payment, Wu Mei demands slutty dressing — reveals they are perfectly matched in mutual transactionalism and rudeness
jokes.explanation: Good payoff on the Pierce/Wu Mei arc. Their immediate rapport as transactional equals — she demands he pay, he demands she dress provocatively, both treat this as fair — confirms Jeff's matchmaking logic. 'You're dressing slutty' as the counter-demand is the kind of line only Pierce would issue as a date prerequisite.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'I guess we could go out to one dinner.' Wu Mei: 'You're paying.' Pierce: 'You're dressing slutty.'
jokes.setup: Pierce and Wu Mei are tentatively agreeing to a date
jokes.punchline: Their negotiation immediately devolves into mutual demands — Wu Mei's is financial, Pierce's is sartorial — establishing them as equals in awfulness
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to Annie's matchmaking. The rapid-fire demand exchange ('You're paying.' / 'You're dressing slutty.') establishes their dynamic in two beats. The parallel structure makes it feel like these two deserve each other.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'How about Mexican?' Wu Mei: 'How about Thai?' Pierce: 'They're like Chinese Mexicans.' Wu Mei: 'Hmm, so true.'
jokes.setup: Pierce and Wu Mei negotiate a restaurant for their date
jokes.punchline: Pierce's racist oversimplification ('Chinese Mexicans') is validated by Wu Mei — a Chinese woman — finding it 'so true,' confirming that she is exactly as Pierce-like as Annie said
jokes.explanation: Smart character-pairing payoff. Wu Mei agreeing with Pierce's racist non-logic is both surprising (a Chinese woman validating racial oversimplification) and the entire point of Annie's matchmaking thesis — they really are alike. The 'Hmm, so true' is Wu Mei's funniest moment.

jokes.text: Troy performing in 'Fiddla Please' — a Fiddler on the Roof adaptation described as an 'all-black production' by Professor Garrity, with Troy singing a hip-hop version of the score.
jokes.setup: Troy mentions he's auditioning for an all-black production of Fiddler on the Roof called 'Fiddla Please'
jokes.punchline: The end tag shows Troy performing it — the title 'Fiddla Please' and the hip-hop/traditional Jewish musical hybrid is the visual and tonal absurdity
jokes.explanation: Fun end-tag joke. 'Fiddla Please' as a title is a good pun/mashup. The concept of a hip-hop Fiddler on the Roof doesn't just exist as dialogue — the tag delivers it, which is a commitment the show doesn't have to make but does. Troy's performance investment is classic.

jokes.text: "Someone drop an old testament beat. / Dreidels."
jokes.setup: Troy is rapping in the Fiddla Please performance and calls for a musical break
jokes.punchline: 'Dreidels.' — the response to 'drop an old testament beat' is the single word 'Dreidels,' which is both the most Jewish possible answer and completely inadequate as a musical direction
jokes.explanation: One-word punchline at maximum economy. 'Dreidels' as a response to 'old testament beat' is funny because it's the most stereotypically Jewish item anyone could name, delivered with total confidence as a musical solution. The gap between the grandeur of 'old testament beat' and the mundanity of 'dreidels' is the whole joke.

tmdb_overview: Jeff is suspicious of Pierce's engagement to a pretty classmate. Troy invents a childhood trauma to impress Britta, and Abed challenges a professor.
insight: Wine episode struggles with tone—54 jokes land at only 72.9, dragged by uneven cringe execution.
